The New York Stock Exchange is getting in on the extended-hours options trading action, with a new early trading session from 7:30 a.m. to 9:25 a.m. ET and a new late trading session from 4 p.m. to 4:15 p.m. ET.

After the Cboe announced on October 15 that it would extend trading hours for options on two dozen stocks and ETFs, the NYSE, owned and operated by (NYSE: ICE), saw little reason not to join the high-leverage party.

Remember, NYSE's parent, the Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) is a publicly traded company, founded and run by CEO Jeff Sprecher. His wife, Kelly Loeffler, serves as the 28th administrator of the U.S. Small Business Administration.

Though Loeffler has no connection to ICE today, she consistently stressed in the past that ICE is a commercial business and not a government-operated entity or a nonprofit trust. In other words, ICE lives, breathes and operates by the rules of free market capitalism. Given that perspective, the NYSE following Cboe down this road of inevitable 24/7 trading makes sense for the company: It's good for business, no matter how volatile it may make markets or how terrible it might be for the humans behind said trading desks.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

Twenty-nine major stocks and funds are available for extended trading, according to CNBC. Nvidia, Bank of America, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust and others are included. Beginning in early December, NYSE, as well as the CBOE on its Cboe BZX Exchange, will extend trading to 23 hours, five days a week.

As the NYSE and Cboe extend their trading hours to almost every hour, Robinhood (HOOD) keeps growing its margin business. Robinhood's margin book hit a record $21.6 billion in Q2 2026, up 127% year over year. That same quarter, the SEC signed off on FINRA's rewrite of its margin rules, which took effect on June 4. The old rule forced anyone making four or more day trades in five business days to hold $25,000 in a margin account. Now $2,000 buys unlimited day trading on margin.

With 24/7 markets and CEO Vlad Tenev pushing hard for continued tokenization and agentic trading, unlimited access with little to no restraint is going to be the future of markets.

(Updates with market moves at the end of the day, and other changes, if any.)

The Nasdaq Composite rose Monday in a relief rally following last week's technology-led sell-off, as traders prepared for earnings reports from big Wall Street names, including Meta Platforms (META).

The tech-heavy Nasdaq climbed 1.1% to 26,430.89, while the S&P 500 gained 0.4% to settle at 7,690.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged down 0.1% to 51,966.03. Most sectors were in the red, led by utilities, while consumer discretionary paced the winners with a 2.7% advance followed by tech's 1.2% gain.

Amazon.com (AMZN) was up 5%, the best performer on the Dow, followed by IBM and chip-making giant Nvidia (NVDA), with Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) also among the index's biggest gainers.

Nvidia said it ran a record-breaking quantum computing simulation on Jupiter, Europe's first exascale supercomputer, allowing researchers to explore and validate magic state cultivation.

Alphabet likely saw "relatively healthy" Google search revenue growth in the third quarter, driven by higher pricing amid solid search volume, Deutsche Bank said Monday.

On the S&P 500, SanDisk (SNDK), Datadog (DDOG) and Marvell Technology (MRVL) were among the biggest gainers.

Ameriprise Financial (AMP) fell 4.1%, among the worst performers on the S&P 500, after BofA Securities downgraded the company's stock to underperform from buy.

Netflix (NFLX) is expected to report quarterly earnings on Tuesday, with Facebook and WhatsApp parent Meta and electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla (TSLA) scheduled to release theirs on Wednesday after market close.

GE Aerospace (GE), Philip Morris International (PM), Thermo Fisher Scientific (TMO), Procter & Gamble (PG) and American Express (AXP) also report this week.

Oppenheimer Asset Management upgraded its S&P 500 full-year earnings outlook, saying the third-quarter reporting season got off to a solid start. The firm continues to expect the index to close 2026 out at 8,100.

"Our expectations are that another better-than expected quarter is in the offing," Oppenheimer Asset Management Chief Investment Strategist John Stoltzfus said in a report Monday. "Given the economic and corporate fundamentals experienced over the course of recent quarters along with watershed innovation that has seen reports of increased adoption of (artificial intelligence) by businesses and consumers, stocks may well have further upside ahead before year-end."

Treasury yields were higher with the 10-year rate up 4.2 basis points at 5.14%, while the two-year rate rose 3.4 basis points to 4.77%.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil advanced 2.1% to $103.56 a barrel in Monday late-afternoon trade, while Brent dropped 0.5% to $109.37.

US President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order to waive key sanctions and tariffs on Russia.

Trump had recently lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping and himself next month to discuss a potential deal to end the Ukraine war, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the discussions.

Spot gold fell 0.6% to $4,140.61 per troy ounce, while silver ticked down 0.1% to $57.25 per ounce.

title: Why CoreWeave's Struggles Could Weigh Down Nvidia's Stock
detail:
Why CoreWeave's Struggles Could Weigh Down Nvidia's Stock
David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 3:29 PM CDT 4 min read
NVDA
CRWV
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV)'s stock crashed last week amid concerns of rising interest rates and its high debt load. CoreWeave has a close relationship with tech giant Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and is a big customer of theirs. Not only that, but Nvidia has also invested billions into CoreWeave, and thus, it has a lot at stake in how the neocloud company does.

Both stocks have been struggling of late, although Nvidia's decline has been much more modest in comparison; it has declined by around 2% over the past month, while CoreWeave's stock is down well over 20%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, things could get worse for Nvidia as concerns related to CoreWeave may cause investors to question how sustainable Nvidia's long-term growth really is, particularly if companies have to scale back investments in artificial intelligence (AI) due to rising interest rates.

Image source: Getty Images.

Nvidia's stock looks cheap, but that's based on future expectations

It may be odd to think that the most highly valued stock on the U.S. markets, Nvidia, is a cheap buy. It has a market cap of around $5.2 trillion, but many growth investors still believe it's a cheap stock to own due to its earnings expectations. Nvidia is trading at a forward price-to-earnings multiple of 25, which is based on how profitable analysts expect the business to be over the coming year.

And when looking at the price-to-earnings-growth multiple, or PEG, then it looks like a downright steal at approximately 0.48. The cutoff for a cheap stock based on PEG, which factors in a company's expected growth over the next five years, is 1.0 -- Nvidia is well below that.

The problem is if anything shakes the confidence in Nvidia's future growth. CoreWeave's problems could be symbolic of that. It's a key customer that also rents out compute power to other businesses. If it runs into problems because of its high debt load and interest costs, investors may become even more concerned about the growth prospects of smaller, riskier businesses that don't have the close relationship with Nvidia that CoreWeave benefits from.

Investors should tread carefully with Nvidia

Nvidia has a terrific business, and it's benefited from considerable investments in AI in recent years. But at the same time, more tech companies are making their own chips and looking to other chipmakers in an effort to cut costs and be less dependent on Nvidia. And rising interest rates may lead to some companies pulling back on capital expenditures.
